la:verb:averto.gloss: to turn away, turn off, avert; to avoid, divert, deviate
senses: to turn away, turn off, avert; to avoid, divert, deviate
to steal, embezzle, appropriate to oneself
la:verb:averto.html:
ā-verto (arch. -vorto; in MSS. also abverto; cf. ab
init.), ti, sum, 3, v. a., to turn something away from a place, to avert, turn off, remove, etc. (opp. adverto).
Lit.
In gen.
Constr. aliquem ab or with the simple abl.; the limit designated by in with acc. (more rarely by ad): ab saxo avortit fluctus ad litus scapham,: Jup. Te volo, uxor, conloqui. Quor ted avortisti? Alc. Est ita ingenium meum: Inimicos semper osa sum optuerier,: (M. Lepidus) Antonio diadema Caesari imponente se avertit,; : aliquid ab oculis,: nos flumina arcemus, dirigimus, avertimus,turn off,; so : quod iter ab Arari Helvetii averterant,had turned aside their march from et saep.: locis seminis ic tum,: Italiā Teucrorum regem,: a ceteris omnium in se oculos,: in comitiorum disceptationem ab lege certamen,: ab hominibus ad deos preces,: se alicui, instead of ab aliquo. .—And poet. with acc.: quo regnum Italiae Libycas averteret oras,. —With dat.: Quod mihi non patrii poterant avertere amici,; so .—Also without an antecedent ab (since this is included in the verb) with in with acc.: in fugam classem, Liv 22, 19, 11: dissipatos in fugam,; hence absol.: mille acies avertit avertetque (sc. in fugam),put to flight,.—
Pass. in mid. signif. with the acc., in the Greek manner, to turn away from: equus fontes avertitur, (cf. the Gr. ἀποστρέφεσθαι τὸ ὕδωρ, and aversari): oppositas impasta avertitur herbas,; .—
As v. n. avertere = se avertere, to turn one's self away, to retire: ob eam causam huc abs te avorti,: ecce avortit,: dixit et avertens roseā cervice refulsit,: tum prora avertit,: avertit et ire in Capitolium coepit,—
To take away, drive away, carry off, steal, embezzle, to appropriate to one's self: pecuniam publicam,: compertum publicam pecuniam avertisse,: aliquid domum tuam,: praedam omnem domum avertebant,: intellexistis innumerabilem frumenti numerum per triennium aversum a re publicā esse ereptumque aratoribus,: auratam Colchis pellem,to carry off,: quattuor a stabulis tauros,: avertere praedas,: carā pisces avertere mensā,.—
Trop.
To turn, divert a person from a course of action, purpose, etc.: accusandi terrores et minae populi opinionem a spe adipiscendi avertunt,: avertant animos a spe recuperandae arcis,: qui mentem optimi viri a defensione meae salutis averterant,: ut nec vobis averteretur a certamine animus,: animum a pietate,: aliquem ab incepto avertit,: a philosophiā,.—
Aliquem, to turn away from one in feeling, i. e. to make averse or disinclined to, to alienate, estrange: legiones abducis a Bruto. Quas? nempe eas, quas ille a C. Antonii scelere avertit et ad rem publicam suā auctoritate traduxit,: ipse Pompeius totum se ab ejus (sc. Caesaris) amicitiā averterat,had quite alienated himself from,: civitates ab alicujus amicitiā,: popularium animos,: futurum, uti totius Galliae animi a se averterentur,: nobis mentem deorum,.—Hence, āver-sus, a, um, P. a.
Turned off or away: aversum hostem videre nemo potuit, turned away, i. e. turned in flight, ; hence, backwards, behind, back ( = a tergo; opp. adversus), distant: et adversus et aversus impudicus es,before and behind,: canities homini semper a priori parte capitis, tum deinde ab aversā,; : ne aversos nostros aggrederentur, fall upon our troops in the rear, Galba ap. : ne aversi ab hoste circumvenirentur,from behind, in the rear,: aversos proterere,: aversi vulnerantur, Auct. B. Alex. 30; 32: aversum ferro transfixit,: aversos boves caudis in speluncam traxit,backwards, (cf. : Aversos caudā traxit in antra boves): aversa hosti porta,: scribit in aversā Picens epigrammata chartā,upon the back of the paper, (cf. : liber scriptus in tergo), and so al.—Trop.: milites aversi a proelio,withdrawn from the battle,. —Subst.: āversum, i, n., the hinder or back part, the back (as subst. only in the plur.): per aversa castrorum receptus est, Ruhnk.: per aversa urbis fugam dederat,: ad aversa insulae, id.

37, 27, 2: aversa montis,: aversa Indiae, the back or remoter parts of India, .—So in adverb. phrase: in aversum, backwards: Cetera animalia in aversum posterioribus pedibus quam prioribus, (Jan, in diversum): collum circum agit (lynx) in aversum, (Jan, in aversum se; Sillig, in adversum). —

Disinclined, alienated, unfavorable, opposed, hostile, averse; constr. with ab, with dat., or absol.
With ab (so most frequently in Cicero): aversus a Musis,: aversus a vero,: turbidi animorum motus, aversi a ratione, et inimicissimi mentis vitaeque tranquillae,: Quintus aversissimo a me animo fuit,; : aversissimus ab istis prodigiis sum,.—
With dat.: aversus mercaturis,: vilicus aversus contubernio,: defensioni aversior, (but acc. to the MSS., adversior seems here to deserve the preference; so Halm; cf. Spald. and Zumpt ad h. l.).—
Absol.: aversa deae mens,: aversa voluntas,: aversos soliti componere amicos,: aversus animus, et saep.: vultus aversior,: aversi animis,.—Adv. not used.

la:noun:avis.html:
ăvis, is, f. (
abl. sing. avi and ave; cf. Müll.; P.; Rhem. Palaem. p. 1374 P.; Neue, Formenl. I. pp. 218, 222; in the lang. of religion, the form avi is most common; v.infra) [cf. Sanscr. vā (which may imply av), to blow (to wave); vis, a bird; Zend, vi; with which Curt. compares οἰ-ωνός, a large bird, and Benfey αἰ-ετός, an eagle].
Lit., a bird; or collect., the winged tribe: Liber captivos avis ferae consimilis est,: videmus novis avibus canere undique silvas,: arguta,: istā enim avi (sc. aquilā) volat nulla vehementius,: ave ad perfugia litorum tendente,; ; ; ; et saep.—In Varr. once of bees: de incredibili earum avium naturā audi,.—A description of birds is found ap. Plin. l; of their habits, ap. and ap. —
Transf.
Esp., in reference to auguries, since the Romans took their omens or auguries from birds (v. augurium and auspicium): post quam avem aspexit templo Anchises, Naev. ap. Prob. ad .—Hence, avis, meton., = omen a sign, omen, portent, freq. with the epithets bona, mala, sinistra ( = bona; v. sinister), adversa, etc.: liquido exeo foras Auspicio avi sinistrā,: ducam legiones meas Avi sinistrā, auspicio liquido atque ex sententiā,: solvere secundo rumore aversāque avi, poët. ap. , where B. and K. read adversā: malā ducis avi domum,with a bad omen,: este bonis avibus visi natoque mihique,; so : di, qui secundis avibus in proelium miserint,: Quā ego hunc amorem mihi esse avi dicam datum?: Hac veniat natalis avi,.—In abl., form ave: tunc ave deceptus falsā,.—
Comically, for a man in the garb of a bird: Sed quae nam illaec est avis, quae huc cum tunicis advenit?.—
Avis alba, v. albus, I. B. 3. e.

la:noun:avus.html:
ăvus (AVS, , also ăvŏs), i, m.
kindr. with Goth. avo, grandmother; old Norse, afi, grandfather; cf. Heb. , āb, father; Chald. , ἀββᾶ; and Engl. abbot
,
a grandfather, grandsire.
Lit.: pater, avus, proavus, abavus, atavus, tritavus,; so ; ; ; ; ; cf. ; ; ; .—Also transf. to animals (cf. 1. avitus, II.), .—
In gen.
Ancestor, forefather, ; ; (15), 174; ; ; ; —
An old man, .

la:verb:avolo.gloss: to fly off or away; flee away
senses: to fly off or away; flee away
la:verb:avolo.html:
ā-vŏlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n.,
to fly forth or away: per aetherias umbras,: auspicanti pullos avolāsse,; .—Hence, of persons, to flee away, to go away quickly, to hasten away (opp. advolare, to flee to): experiar certe, ut hinc avolem,: avolat ipse,: citatis equls avolant Romam,; (al. advolat).—So of dying: Critoni non persuasi me hinc avolaturum,that I shall flee from this world,.—Of the vanishing of pleasure: Fluit voluptas corporis et prima quaequo avolat,.

la:adj:avius.html:
ā-vĭus, a, um, adj.
via
,
that is out of the way, remote, out of the right way; also, untrodden, unfrequented, solitary, lonely, etc. (while devius signifies leading from the right way; and invius, having no way, pathless; in the poets and histt. freq.).
Lit.
Silvani lucus extra murum est avius, : Avia Pieridum peragro loca, nullius ante Trita solo,: nemora avia,: virgulta,: montes,: aviis itineribus,through by-ways,: cujus (Caesaris) sibi species itinere avio occurrisset,: solitudines,: avia commeatibus loca,.—Also,
Subst.: āvĭum, ii, n., a by-way, a desert, wilderness; in a pun with avium, from avis: hunc avium dulcedo ducit ad avium, Auct. ad .—More freq. in plur.: āvĭa, ōrum: avia cursu Dum sequor, et notā excedo regione viarum,: per avia ac derupta,: per avia, Ov M. 1, 701; 2, 205.—So with gen.: avia

vinerum, : nemorum,: saltuum,. 68: Oceani,: Armeniae,.—

Poet., of persons, wandering, straying: Continuo in montes sese avius abdidit altos,.—
Trop.: Avius a verā longe ratione vagaris,astray,; ; ; 3, 463: init nunc avia coepto Consilia,i. e. leading away from the undertaking,.

la:verb:avoco.gloss: to call off or away, withdraw, divert, remove, separate, turn
senses: to call off or away, withdraw, divert, remove, separate, turn
to distract or divert someone's attention
to divert by cheering; cheer, amuse, occupy
la:verb:avoco.html:
ā-vŏco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (arch.
inf., AVOCARIER, C. I. L. I. p. 198), to call off or away.
In gen.: partem exercitūs ad bellum,: pubem in arcem praesidio armisque obtinendam,: Consul ab omnibus magistratibus et comitiatum et contionem avocare potest. Messala ap. .—With dat. (for ab aliquo): nec avocare alius alii posset, si contionem habere volunt, Messala ap. .— Trop.: a rebus occultis avocare philosophiam,: ut (orator) a propriis personis et temporibus avocet controversiam,: quibusdam ad Antiochum multitudinis animos avocantibus,.—
Esp.
To call one off from an action, purpose, wish, etc., i. e. to withdraw, divert, turn, remove, separate (the usual signif. of the word): aliquem ab aliquā re voluptas avocat,: si te laus adlicere ad recte faciendum non potest, ne metus quidem a foedissimis factis potest avocare?: aliquem ab alicujus conjunctione,: quos jam aetas a proeliis avocabat,: senectus avocat a rebus gerendis,; so : qui omnino avocent a philosophiā,; hos a bello avocas, : avocat a curā vocis ille adfectus,; .—
To withdraw the attention, to distract, divert.
To withdraw by interrupting, to interrupt, hinder: multum distringebar frigidis negotiis, quae simul et avocant animum et comminuunt,.—
To divert by cheering, to divert, cheer, amuse: ab iis quae avocant abductus, et liber et mihi relictus,; hence, se, to divert, entertain one's self, ; and pass. with mid. sense: illic avocare et illic lude, * .—
In the Lat. of the jurists = revocare, to reclaim, recall: partem ejus, quod in fraudem datum esset,; so, possessionem,; also with dat. (for ab aliquo): non potest avocari ei res,.—
Trop.: factum,to revoke, disavow,: arma,to make a feint in fighting,.

senses: eager, enthusiastic, desiring, desirous; lustful, passionate
la:adj:avidus.html:
ăvĭdus, a, um, adj.
1. aveo
,
longing eagerly for something (either lawful or unlawful),desirous, eager, earnest, greedy (diff. from avarus, q. v.).
In gen., constr. with gen., in with acc., dat., or absol.
With gen.: cibi,: Romani semper appetentes gloriae praeter ceteras gentes atque avidi laudis,: festinatio victoriae avida,; so, potentiae, honoris, divitiarum,: avidissimus privatae gratiae, id. H. Fr. (Orat. Cottae ad Popul. p. 245 Gerl.): turba avida novarum rerum,: avidus poenae (sc. sumendae),: libidinum,: futuri, et saep.: belli gerundi,: malefaciundi, id. H. Fr. ap. (p. 251, n. 116 Gerl.): avidior properandi, Gerl.: videndi, et saep.— Poet. with inf. (inst. of gen. of gerund.): avidi committere pugnam,: cognoscere amantem,: Chaos innumeros avidum confundere mundos,—A. more remote gen. relation is found in Lucr.: Humanum genus est avidum nimis auricularum,in respect of,.—
With in with acc.: avida in novas res ingenia,: avidae in direptiones manus,.—*
With dat.: servorum manus subitis avidae,.—
Absol. and transf. to inanimate things: ita sunt avidae (aures meae), etc.,: avidi cursus frena retentat equi,: avidae libidines,: amor,: cor,: pectus,: amplexus,.—
Esp
Eager for gain, avaricious, covetous, greedy of money, = avarus: me dices avidum esse hominem,; ; ; : Sed habet patrem quendam avidum, miserum atque aridum,: divitiasque Conduplicant avidi,: aliquantum ad rem avidior,: grati animi, non appetentis, non avidi signa proferri perutile est,; : avidae manus heredis,—
Eager for food, hungry, greedy, voracious, gluttonous: Avidos vicinum funus et aegros Exanimat,: convivae,: Noli avidus esse in omni epulatione, * .— Poet.: Efficit ut largis avidum mare fluminis undis,insatiable,: Exitio est avidum mare nautis,: morbus,: manus Mortis,: ignis,; : flammae,: morsus, et saep.—
In Lucr. of space as swallowing up objects, wide, large, vast: Inde avidei partem montes silvaeque ferarum Possedere,: avido complexu quem tenet aether ; so .—Adv., eagerly, greedily, etc.
Anteclass. form ăvĭdĭter: invadere pocula, Val. Antias ap. ; so App.: merum ventri ingurgitare, Met. 4, p. 145, 27.—
Class. form ăvĭdē: ab ludis animus atque aures avent avide exspectantes mentium, Enn. ap. Müll. (Trag. v. 71 Vahl.); : adripere Graecas litteras,: adpetere aliquid,: exspectare aliquid,; : jam bibit avide,: pransus,— Comp.: avidius se in voluptates mergere,: procurrere,: avidius vino ciboque corpora onerant,: vesci,.—Sup.: avidissime exspectare aliquid,: credere aliquid,: adprehendere palmam,.

la:verb:aveo.gloss: to desire, wish or long for, crave, be eager
senses: to desire, wish or long for, crave, be eager
la:verb:aveo.html:
ăvĕo, ēre, v. a.
from Sanscr. av, to love, to wish; to satisfy one's self, to be content, to do or fare well
,
to wish, desire earnestly, to long for, crave (syn.: volo, cupio): avere nihil aliud est quam cupere, Paul. ex Müll.: ab ludis animus atque aures avent Avide exspectantes nuntium, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 70 Vahl.).—Constr. with inf., acc., and absol.
With inf.: te imitari aveo,: Illud in his quoque te rebus cognoscere avemus,: res exponere,: rationem reddere,: discedere aventes,: Non est mihi tempus aventi Ponere signa novis praeceptis,; : propiusque accedere aventi figere pectora,: valde aveo scire quid agas,; ; ; ; : Jam mens praetrepidans avet vagari,: avet (ara) spargier agno,: ipsum L. Paulum omnium oculi conspicere urbem curru ingredientem avent,; ; : avebat animus antire statimque memorare exitus,; .—
With acc.: quia semper aves quod abest, praesentia temnis,; so ; : parto, quod avebas,: aveo genus legationis ut, etc., (acc. to conj. of Gronov.; so B. and K.; v. Orell. ad h. l.); .—
Absol.: Et mora, quae fluvios passim refrenat aventes,which restrains the eager river,, where Lachm. and Munro read euntīs: Talem dira sibi scelerisque dolique ministram Quaerit avens,; .—
Avens = libens, Laev. ap. .—ăventer, adv., eagerly, earnestly (post - class.), ; v. and 19.

la:noun:avunculus.html:
ăvuncŭlus (AVOMCVLVS and AVONCLVS, Fabr. Gloss. p. 227, a), i, m.dim.
avus; cf. Lith. avynas, uncle
,
a mother's brother, maternal uncle (a brother of the father, patruus).
Lit.
In gen., ; ; ; ; : uxor patrui vel avunculi,; ; cf. P.—Hence,
Esp.
Avunculus magnus, a grandmother's brother (aviae frater), great-uncle, ; ; ; .—
Avunculus major, a brother of the great-grandmother, greatgreat-uncle (proaviae frater), Dig. l. l. (in l. l., proavunculus).—
Avunculus maximus, a brother of the great-greatgrandmother (abaviae frater), Dig. l. l. (in l. l., abavunculus).—In the histt. sometimes avunculus major = avunculus magnus, brother of the grandmother, ; ; ; and avunculus absol. = avunculus major, ; ; .—
Transf., the husband of the mother's sister, .

la:noun:aviditas.gloss: An eagerness for something, avidity, longing, desire; covetousness, greed, avarice; gluttony, hunger
senses: An eagerness for something, avidity, longing, desire; covetousness, greed, avarice; gluttony, hunger
la:noun:aviditas.html:
ăvĭdĭtas, ātis, f.
avidus
,
an eagerness for something (either lawful or unlawful), avidity, longing, vehement desire.
In gen.: habeo senectuti magnam gratiam, quae mihi sermonis aviditatem auxit, potionis et cibi sustulit,: aviditas legendi,: suscipere verbum cum omni aviditate,: gloriae,: pecuniae,: rapiendi per occasionem triumphi,: imperandi,: vini,: ad cibos,.—In plur.: bestiolarum aviditates,: feminarum,.—
Esp.
Eagerness for money, covetousness, avarice: Inhaeret etiam aviditas, desidia, injuria, etc.,: (justitia) eas res spernit et neglegit, ad quas plerique inflammati aviditate rapiuntur,: utrumque incredibile est, et Roscium quicquam per aviditatem appetīsse et Fannium quicquam per bonitatem amisisse, (B. and K., avaritiam).—
Eagerness in eating, appetite: lactuca in cibis aviditatem incitat inhibetque eadem,; so, aviditatem excitare,: facere,; .

la:noun:avaritia.gloss: A greedy desire for possessions or gain; avarice, greed, greediness, covetousness, rapacity.
senses: A greedy desire for possessions or gain; avarice, greed, greediness, covetousness, rapacity.
la:noun:avaritia.html:
ăvārĭtĭa, ae, f.
avarus
,
a greedy desire for possessions, greediness, avarice, covetousness (opp. abstinentia, ; periphrastically, pecuniae cupiditas,; syn.: aviditas, cupido).
Lit.: Est autem avaritia opinatio vehemens de pecuniā, quasi valde expetenda sit, inhaerens et penitus insita,: avaritia est injuriosa appetitio alienorum, Auct. ad : avaritiam si tollere voltis, mater ejus est tollenda luxuries,: avaritia hians et imminens,a gaping and eager avarice,: pueris talorum nucumque avaritia est: viris auri argentique et urbium,: avaritiae (sc. nimiae parsimoniae) singulos increpans, et saep.—In plur.: omnes avaritiae,every kind of selfishness,. —
Transf., of eagerness for food, gluttony: Quam siquis avidus poscit escam avariter, Decipitur in transennā avaritia sua,.—Trop.: avaritia gloriae, eager desire for renown or glory, .

la:adj:avarus.html:
ăvārus, a, um, adj. (
gen. plur. fem. avarūm, dub.; Speng., aurum) [1. aveo, ], eagerly desirous of something, esp. of possessions, avaricious, covetous, greedy (opp. largus, Quadrig. ap. : avarum et avidum ita discernuntur: avarum semper in reprehensione est; avidum autem malis aliquando, aliquando bonis adjungitur,; v. II.; syn.: avidus, cupidus, tenax, sordidus).
Lit.: meretrix,, and ; cf.: Carmine formosae, pretio capiuntur avarae,: leno,: avarus et furax homo,: semper avarus eget,: quantum discordet parcus avaro,.—With gen.: publicae pecuniae,: caedis, et saep.—Poet. transf. to inanimate things: fuge litus avarum, ( = avarorum, Serv.): Troja, i. e. with reference to the perjured avarice of Laomedon, (cf.: perjura Troja,; ): fraus,: spes,: venter,: mare,: Acheron. : ignis,—
Transf., in the poets sometimes without the access. idea of reproach: Graiis praeter laudem nullius avaris, eager only for glory, Hor.A.P.324: agricola,.—Comp.: avariores magistratus,: ruberes, Viveret in terris te si quis avarior uno,. —Sup.: homo avarissime et spurcissime,.—Adv., covetously, greedily, avariciously, etc.
Ante-class. form ăvārĭter, Cato and Quadrig. ap. : ingurgitare,. —Of gluttony: si quis avidus poscit escam avariter,; cf. avaritia, II.—
Class. form ăvārē: avare pretium statui arti meae,: aliquid facere,; : superbe avareque imperitare victis,; cf. .—Comp., more eagerly, more greedily: avarius exigere opus,.—Sup.: avarissime horas suas servare,.

la:noun:avarus.html:
ăvārus, a, um, adj. (
gen. plur. fem. avarūm, dub.; Speng., aurum) [1. aveo, ], eagerly desirous of something, esp. of possessions, avaricious, covetous, greedy (opp. largus, Quadrig. ap. : avarum et avidum ita discernuntur: avarum semper in reprehensione est; avidum autem malis aliquando, aliquando bonis adjungitur,; v. II.; syn.: avidus, cupidus, tenax, sordidus).
Lit.: meretrix,, and ; cf.: Carmine formosae, pretio capiuntur avarae,: leno,: avarus et furax homo,: semper avarus eget,: quantum discordet parcus avaro,.—With gen.: publicae pecuniae,: caedis, et saep.—Poet. transf. to inanimate things: fuge litus avarum, ( = avarorum, Serv.): Troja, i. e. with reference to the perjured avarice of Laomedon, (cf.: perjura Troja,; ): fraus,: spes,: venter,: mare,: Acheron. : ignis,—
Transf., in the poets sometimes without the access. idea of reproach: Graiis praeter laudem nullius avaris, eager only for glory, Hor.A.P.324: agricola,.—Comp.: avariores magistratus,: ruberes, Viveret in terris te si quis avarior uno,. —Sup.: homo avarissime et spurcissime,.—Adv., covetously, greedily, avariciously, etc.
Ante-class. form ăvārĭter, Cato and Quadrig. ap. : ingurgitare,. —Of gluttony: si quis avidus poscit escam avariter,; cf. avaritia, II.—
Class. form ăvārē: avare pretium statui arti meae,: aliquid facere,; : superbe avareque imperitare victis,; cf. .—Comp., more eagerly, more greedily: avarius exigere opus,.—Sup.: avarissime horas suas servare,.

la:verb:aveho.html:
ā-vĕho (in MSS. abvĕho; v. ab
init.), vexi, vectum, 3, v. a. (avexti = avexisti, ), to carry off or away, to bear off (of chariots, ships, horses, etc.; v. veho; class., but perh. not in Cic.; syn. aufero): Pl. Rogas? Quine eam hinc avexti? La. Non avexi, ; : aliquem a patriā,: ex Samo,: Athenis,: domum,: in finitimas urbes,: in alias terras,; so ; : ad aras,.—With the simple acc.: penitusque alias avexerat oras, Wagn.: equites Aegyptum avexit,.—Pass., to be carried away, to ride away, to depart: avectus (sc. equo) ab suis,: creditis avectos hostes?

la:verb:avello.html:
ā-vello, velli or vulsi, vulsum or volsum, 3, v. a. (
pluperf. avellerat, ; perf. avulsi, ), to tear off or away, to pull or rend off (syn.: abripio, eximo).
In gen. (class.): avellere tigna trabesque,to tear away planks and beams,: avolsaque saxa Montibus,the rocks rent from the mountains,: avolsum umeris caput,; so ; : avolsos silices a montibus altis,: avolsus radicibus oculus,: poma ex arboribus, si cruda sunt, vix avelluntur; si matura et cocta, decidunt,; : Cum ripa simul avolsos ferat Aufidus acer,; : Avellit frondes,: summitatem frondium ejus avulsit,: Ex eā avolsa postea Therasia,: Euboea avolsa Boeotiae,.—
Esp.
To take away by force, to tear away: rus ab aliquo,: pretium alicui,: fatale sacrato avellere templo Palladium,: fundum emptori,; : avellamus eum ad nos,; so of carrying off the bride, Ellis.—
To separate from something by pulling, to part, to remove: aliquem de matris complexu avellere atque abstrahere,: ab uberibus avellere,to wean,: ut sperem posse (eum) avelli,: Non potes avelli! simul, ah, simul ibimus, inquit,: complexu avolsus Iuli,: ut avellerentur castris,: se, to tear one's self away, .— And in pass. without the notion of violence, to withdraw: Et ipse avulsus est ab eis, Tisch.—Trop.: aliquem a tanto errore,.

la:noun:Avernus.html:
Ăvernus, a, um, adj., = ἄορνος.
Without birds: loca,where no birds can live, on account of the pestiferous exhalations,; : aestus,the vapor of Avernus,.—But esp. Avernus lacus or absol. Avernus, Lake Avernus, near Cumœ, Puteoli, and Baiœ, almost entirely enclosed by steep and wooded hills (now Lago Averno), whose deadly exhalations killed the birds flying over it; therefore the myth placed near it the entrance to the lower world, ; ; ; ; cf. Mann. Ital. I. p. 718 sq.; Heyne, Excurs. II. ad .—The renowned Cumæan Sibyl also dwelt in a grotto near it.—Poet., the lower world, the infernal regions, ; ; —Also = Acheron: pigri sulcator Averni,.—Personified as a deity, acc. to .—Hence,
Another adj.: ăvernus, a, um.
Belonging to Lake Avernus: luci,; : valles,: freta,Lake Avernus,.—Also absol.: ăverna, ōrum, n. (sc. loca), ; ; .—
Of or belonging to the infernal regions: stagna,: tenebrae,: Juno,i. e. Proserpina,; (cf.: Juno inferna,).

la:adj:avitus.html:
ăvītus, a, um, adj.
avus
,
of or belonging to a grandfather, coming from a grandfather, ancestral.
Lit.: paternae atque avitae possessiones,: bona paterna et avita,: res patrita et avita,: patrita illa et avita philosophia,: avitus ac patritus mos, Varr. ap. : leges avitae et patritae,: hospitium,: divitiae,; so, res,: quae (pallium, sudarium etc.) palam soles habere tamquam avita,: solium,; : fundus,: cellae,: regnum,; : sanguis, Prep. 3, 19, 37: nomen,: umbrae,: nobilitas,: spes, et saep.—
Transf. to animals: asinus fortitudinem celeritatemque avitam refert,: color,.—In gen., very old or ancient: merum,.—Comp. and sup. not found; cf. Neue, Formenl. II. p. 230.—* Adv.: ăvītë;, from ancient times, dub.

la:other:Aventinus.html:
Ăventīnus, i, m.
(Sc. mons.) The Aventine, one of the seven hills of Rome, extending from the Palatine to the Cœlian Mount; until the reign of Ancus Marcius, without the city proper, ; ; . The origin of the name is uncertain; acc. to , it was named from Aventinus, an Alban king buried there; other etymologies are given by Müll.; cf. , where, beside the etymologies given and referred to, another is given from Varro; cf. Creuz, Antiq. p. 23 sq.; Smith, Dict. Antiq.—Neutr.: Aventī-num, i, and 5; 21, 62, 8.— Hence,
The adjj.,
ăventīnus, a, um, of Mount Aventine: cacumen,: jugum,: arx,: humus,: Remus, because he consulted the auspices there (therefore its summit was called Remuria; v. Remurinus),: Diana, because she had there an ancient and very distinguished temple,; cf. ; ; .—
ăven-tīnensis (Fest. s. v. nesi, p. 165 Müll.) or ăventīnĭensis (), e, of or belonging to Mount Aventine: Diana, who had a temple upon the Aventine Hill —
A son of Hercules, .

la:verb:averto#2.html:
ā-verto (arch. -vorto; in MSS. also abverto; cf. ab
init.), ti, sum, 3, v. a., to turn something away from a place, to avert, turn off, remove, etc. (opp. adverto).
Lit.
In gen.
Constr. aliquem ab or with the simple abl.; the limit designated by in with acc. (more rarely by ad): ab saxo avortit fluctus ad litus scapham,: Jup. Te volo, uxor, conloqui. Quor ted avortisti? Alc. Est ita ingenium meum: Inimicos semper osa sum optuerier,: (M. Lepidus) Antonio diadema Caesari imponente se avertit,; : aliquid ab oculis,: nos flumina arcemus, dirigimus, avertimus,turn off,; so : quod iter ab Arari Helvetii averterant,had turned aside their march from et saep.: locis seminis ic tum,: Italiā Teucrorum regem,: a ceteris omnium in se oculos,: in comitiorum disceptationem ab lege certamen,: ab hominibus ad deos preces,: se alicui, instead of ab aliquo. .—And poet. with acc.: quo regnum Italiae Libycas averteret oras,. —With dat.: Quod mihi non patrii poterant avertere amici,; so .—Also without an antecedent ab (since this is included in the verb) with in with acc.: in fugam classem, Liv 22, 19, 11: dissipatos in fugam,; hence absol.: mille acies avertit avertetque (sc. in fugam),put to flight,.—
Pass. in mid. signif. with the acc., in the Greek manner, to turn away from: equus fontes avertitur, (cf. the Gr. ἀποστρέφεσθαι τὸ ὕδωρ, and aversari): oppositas impasta avertitur herbas,; .—
As v. n. avertere = se avertere, to turn one's self away, to retire: ob eam causam huc abs te avorti,: ecce avortit,: dixit et avertens roseā cervice refulsit,: tum prora avertit,: avertit et ire in Capitolium coepit,—
To take away, drive away, carry off, steal, embezzle, to appropriate to one's self: pecuniam publicam,: compertum publicam pecuniam avertisse,: aliquid domum tuam,: praedam omnem domum avertebant,: intellexistis innumerabilem frumenti numerum per triennium aversum a re publicā esse ereptumque aratoribus,: auratam Colchis pellem,to carry off,: quattuor a stabulis tauros,: avertere praedas,: carā pisces avertere mensā,.—
Trop.
To turn, divert a person from a course of action, purpose, etc.: accusandi terrores et minae populi opinionem a spe adipiscendi avertunt,: avertant animos a spe recuperandae arcis,: qui mentem optimi viri a defensione meae salutis averterant,: ut nec vobis averteretur a certamine animus,: animum a pietate,: aliquem ab incepto avertit,: a philosophiā,.—
Aliquem, to turn away from one in feeling, i. e. to make averse or disinclined to, to alienate, estrange: legiones abducis a Bruto. Quas? nempe eas, quas ille a C. Antonii scelere avertit et ad rem publicam suā auctoritate traduxit,: ipse Pompeius totum se ab ejus (sc. Caesaris) amicitiā averterat,had quite alienated himself from,: civitates ab alicujus amicitiā,: popularium animos,: futurum, uti totius Galliae animi a se averterentur,: nobis mentem deorum,.—Hence, āver-sus, a, um, P. a.
Turned off or away: aversum hostem videre nemo potuit, turned away, i. e. turned in flight, ; hence, backwards, behind, back ( = a tergo; opp. adversus), distant: et adversus et aversus impudicus es,before and behind,: canities homini semper a priori parte capitis, tum deinde ab aversā,; : ne aversos nostros aggrederentur, fall upon our troops in the rear, Galba ap. : ne aversi ab hoste circumvenirentur,from behind, in the rear,: aversos proterere,: aversi vulnerantur, Auct. B. Alex. 30; 32: aversum ferro transfixit,: aversos boves caudis in speluncam traxit,backwards, (cf. : Aversos caudā traxit in antra boves): aversa hosti porta,: scribit in aversā Picens epigrammata chartā,upon the back of the paper, (cf. : liber scriptus in tergo), and so al.—Trop.: milites aversi a proelio,withdrawn from the battle,. —Subst.: āversum, i, n., the hinder or back part, the back (as subst. only in the plur.): per aversa castrorum receptus est, Ruhnk.: per aversa urbis fugam dederat,: ad aversa insulae, id.

37, 27, 2: aversa montis,: aversa Indiae, the back or remoter parts of India, .—So in adverb. phrase: in aversum, backwards: Cetera animalia in aversum posterioribus pedibus quam prioribus, (Jan, in diversum): collum circum agit (lynx) in aversum, (Jan, in aversum se; Sillig, in adversum). —

Disinclined, alienated, unfavorable, opposed, hostile, averse; constr. with ab, with dat., or absol.
With ab (so most frequently in Cicero): aversus a Musis,: aversus a vero,: turbidi animorum motus, aversi a ratione, et inimicissimi mentis vitaeque tranquillae,: Quintus aversissimo a me animo fuit,; : aversissimus ab istis prodigiis sum,.—
With dat.: aversus mercaturis,: vilicus aversus contubernio,: defensioni aversior, (but acc. to the MSS., adversior seems here to deserve the preference; so Halm; cf. Spald. and Zumpt ad h. l.).—
Absol.: aversa deae mens,: aversa voluntas,: aversos soliti componere amicos,: aversus animus, et saep.: vultus aversior,: aversi animis,.—Adv. not used.

la:noun:aversio.html:
āversĭo, ōnis, f.
id.
.
a turning away; only in the adverb. phrases,
Ex aversione, from behind: illi de praesidio insecuti ex aversione legatos jugulārunt, Auct. B. Hisp. 22 Moeb.—
In the Latin of the jurists: per aversionem or aversione emere, vendere, locare, etc., to buy, sell, etc., something, with a turning away, turned away, i. e. without accurate reckoning, in the gross, by the lot, ; ; ; 19, 2, 36; 14, 1, 1 al.—
In rhet., a turning away, a figure by which the orator turns the attention of his hearers from the theme before them, a kind of apostrophe (e. g. ; ; ), ; Aquil. Rom. 9, p. 102 Ruhnk. Frotsch.—
Trop., aversion, loathing (post-class.): non metu mortis se patriam deserere, sed Deorum coactum aversione, Dictys, Bell. Troj. 4, 18: aversione stomachorum di laborant,.

la:verb:aversor#2.html:
āversor, ātus, 1,
v. dep. freq. [id.], to turn one's self from, to turn away (from displeasure, contempt, loathing, shame, etc.).
In gen.: nulla vis tormentorum acerrimorum praetermittitur; aversari advocati et jam vix ferre posse,: haerere homo, aversari, rubere,—
Esp.: aliquem or aliquid, to turn away a person or thing from one's self, to send away, repulse, reject, refuse, decline, shun, avoid: filium (consul) aversatus,i. e. not permitting his presence, Drak.: afflictum non aversatus amicum,: principes Syracusanorum,: aversatur [dicentem], Halm: petentes,; ; : preces,: effeminatas artes, Schwarz; so, crimina,: honorem,: sermonem,: adulationes, Oud.: latum clavum,: imperium,: scelus,.—With inf.: aversati sunt proelium facere, declined, Auct. B. Hisp. 14.!*? Pass.: vultu notare aversato,.

To turn, divert a person from a course of action, purpose, etc.: accusandi terrores et minae populi opinionem a spe adipiscendi avertunt,: avertant animos a spe recuperandae arcis,: qui mentem optimi viri a defensione meae salutis averterant,: ut nec vobis averteretur a certamine animus,: animum a pietate,: aliquem ab incepto avertit,: a philosophiā,.—
Aliquem, to turn away from one in feeling, i. e. to make averse or disinclined to, to alienate, estrange: legiones abducis a Bruto. Quas? nempe eas, quas ille a C. Antonii scelere avertit et ad rem publicam suā auctoritate traduxit,: ipse Pompeius totum se ab ejus (sc. Caesaris) amicitiā averterat,had quite alienated himself from,: civitates ab alicujus amicitiā,: popularium animos,: futurum, uti totius Galliae animi a se averterentur,: nobis mentem deorum,.—Hence, āver-sus, a, um, P. a.
Turned off or away: aversum hostem videre nemo potuit, turned away, i. e. turned in flight, ; hence, backwards, behind, back ( = a tergo; opp. adversus), distant: et adversus et aversus impudicus es,before and behind,: canities homini semper a priori parte capitis, tum deinde ab aversā,; : ne aversos nostros aggrederentur, fall upon our troops in the rear, Galba ap. : ne aversi ab hoste circumvenirentur,from behind, in the rear,: aversos proterere,: aversi vulnerantur, Auct. B. Alex. 30; 32: aversum ferro transfixit,: aversos boves caudis in speluncam traxit,backwards, (cf. : Aversos caudā traxit in antra boves): aversa hosti porta,: scribit in aversā Picens epigrammata chartā,upon the back of the paper, (cf. : liber scriptus in tergo), and so al.—Trop.: milites aversi a proelio,withdrawn from the battle,. —Subst.: āversum, i, n., the hinder or back part, the back (as subst. only in the plur.): per aversa castrorum receptus est, Ruhnk.: per aversa urbis fugam dederat,: ad aversa insulae, id.

37, 27, 2: aversa montis,: aversa Indiae, the back or remoter parts of India, .—So in adverb. phrase: in aversum, backwards: Cetera animalia in aversum posterioribus pedibus quam prioribus, (Jan, in diversum): collum circum agit (lynx) in aversum, (Jan, in aversum se; Sillig, in adversum). —

Disinclined, alienated, unfavorable, opposed, hostile, averse; constr. with ab, with dat., or absol.
With ab (so most frequently in Cicero): aversus a Musis,: aversus a vero,: turbidi animorum motus, aversi a ratione, et inimicissimi mentis vitaeque tranquillae,: Quintus aversissimo a me animo fuit,; : aversissimus ab istis prodigiis sum,.—
With dat.: aversus mercaturis,: vilicus aversus contubernio,: defensioni aversior, (but acc. to the MSS., adversior seems here to deserve the preference; so Halm; cf. Spald. and Zumpt ad h. l.).—
Absol.: aversa deae mens,: aversa voluntas,: aversos soliti componere amicos,: aversus animus, et saep.: vultus aversior,: aversi animis,.—Adv. not used.
